newsitem.title: JAPAN: E. Asian Grain - Japan to buy ahead of USDA report.
newsitem.headline: E. Asian Grain - Japan to buy ahead of USDA report.

text.p: Japanese grain importers will return to the market this week without waiting for the USDA stocks report due out later today in line with lower premiums caused by soft trans-Pacific freight rates, traders said on Monday.
"Local feed makers are now showing interest in buying U.S. corn. Japanese buyers will return to the market this week," a corn trader in Tokyo said.
"U.S. corn premiums continued to ease in line with a drop in freight rates. Local buyers were sidelined as they wanted to confirm the freight's bottom," a corn trader at a major trade house added.
Nearby freight rates on the U.S. Gulf/Japan route reached about $20 a tonne last week compared with $23 in June. It reached below $19 last week as newly-built Panamax-sized ships entered the market.
The Japanese were buying ahead of the 1230 GMT release of the U.S. Agriculture Department's (USDA) grain and soybean stocks report.
Japanese importers had covered over 60 percent of their January/March requirement for U.S. corn.
Premiums for U.S. corn were currently quoted at between 98 and 99 cents a bushel on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) March contract, the traders said.

Japan's soybean crushers will launch their import programme for U.S. soybean this week after they agreed with local feed makers over local soymeal prices for October/December 1996 deliveries, dealers said.
Local soybean crushers and feed makers agreed to set soymeal prices at about 43,000 yen a tonne in the fourth quarter of 1996 against 41,000 yen in the July/September period, the traders said.
Japanese importers have also purchased more than 30 percent of their U.S. soybean needs for November shipment.
"We'd like to cover all November requirements soon," the purchase official of a major Japanese edible oil company said.
Taiwanese buyers are also expected to hold four tenders for up to 104,000 tonnes of U.S. soybeans and 88,000 tonnes of U.S. corn this week, traders said.

The state-owned Taiwan Sugar Corp will probably tender for a combined shipment of 18,000 tonnes of No.2 U.S. corn and 12,000 tonnes of No.2 U.S. soybeans. Delivery date from the U.S. Gulf is from October 25 to November 10.
Taiwan's Hui Shung group also plans to place a tender for a combined shipment of 38,000-tonnes of U.S. soybeans and 16,000 tonnes of U.S. corn, traders said.
Delivery is from November 10 to 25 from the U.S. Gulf or November 26 to December 9 from the Pacific Northwest, they said.

The Breakfast Soybean Procurement Association Taichung group was seen placing a tender for a 54,000-tonne shipment of U.S. soybeans, they added. Delivery is from December 26 to January 9 from the Gulf or January 10 to 24 from the Pacific Northwest.
Grain traders said last week Taiwan's FGEP corn buying group will return to the market for a 54,000-tonne shipment of U.S. corn.

"The corn still looks bearish for the nearby harvest season and no serious frost is expected," an executive at Taiwan's Formosa Oilseeds said. Formosa Oilseeds is a key buyer in Taiwan's Members Feed Industry Group.

In Seoul, South Korean grain buyers were expected to continue to stay on the sidelines this week due to the bearish outlook for grain prices, traders said. Wheat buyers from the Philippines will also sit it out.
"Our target price for corn purchases is moving lower to $2.80-$2.90 per bushel from $3.00 based on December futures in the Chicago Board of Trade," a trader with Cheiljedang Corp said.
"After the Korean Thanksgiving holiday, most buyers appeared to take a wait-and-see attitude as corn prices are expected to fall further," the Cheiljedang trader said.

"We are planning to buy our requirements for November shipment by mid-October," a senior official with Sam Yang Foods Co Ltd said. "However we are slightly nervous about a shortage of soybean supply for upcoming shipments. It will make soybean offer prices for November shipment to go up."
